doc.title: Clay Jenkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 18, 2016

title: State of jazz and jazz education today
summary: He is torn about jazz school costs but impressed by his students, who respect the legacy and play hard music well.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Okay. Jazz in academia. Every once in a while your favorite topic — it seems to, every couple of years I think some critic will write jazz is dead. You know the jazz is dead article. And they cite the abysmal record sales and the club scene. But on the other hand, you have jazz in almost every academic institution in the country and you go to Jazz Education Network, those conferences, and do you have a sort of a perspective on the state of jazz?

Yeah. I mean kids that spend a lot of money in jazz school, I’m kind of torn about that because there’s not a lot of work. It’s a really hard living. It’s really hard to make a living just playing. And so kids kind of write and play, or write, play and teach. And now they’re talking about, at Eastman we’re starting to talk about having classes to write music for games and that kind of stuff. So I mean just finding ways to be more versatile. On the other hand, my kids, and I have lovely, lovely people as students, they’re just the best, they’re great kids. They’re very respectful. And they’re very respectful of the legacy and then they bring in this new stuff. And lately the stuff they’ve been bringing in, I just love the stuff they’ve been bringing in. Years ago some of it felt like sort of self-involved and hard to understand. They were real hard meters and it was hard to play. And we needed that. Because now the meters don’t sound so hard, the odd meters, and our kids, especially just this year, they’ve brought in stuff and played for me and I just, wow, I really like it and it’s been really inspirational. So I don’t know where it’s going in terms of the business, but I certainly think it’s growing in terms of the players. Because all I know is my students but they’re very respectful of the legacy. They never say, “I don’t want to play ‘Gone with the Wind.’” They’re all about that stuff. And I have them study older players like Louis Armstrong and Sweets, and I tell them I don’t want you to necessarily play like that but I want you to have them in your playing. That’s the way we approach it. Professionally every once in a while for a recording session they may be called on to play just like Sweets Edison and that’ll pay off. But that’s not the essence of what I’m trying to do. I’m trying to get Sweets Edison in their playing. Because he wasn’t in mine at first. That was a hole I had to fill. So my students have been so respectful of that, but then surging ahead and they learn really fast. They’re so far ahead of where I was when I was their age. It’s not even funny. They’re so far ahead. I couldn’t play like my kids play when I was a junior in college. Nowhere close. I couldn’t play the way some of them play when I was out on the road with Kenton. Nowhere close. They play much better. So I think it’s accessibility or they’ve learned how to absorb better or

— they’re playing really hard music really well. So I think the music can’t do anything but grow and germinate and be better. I’m not pessimistic about it. The business, yes. But they’ll find a way. Because they were saying that when I was coming out of college. “Oh yeah, you’re not going to make a living doing that.” But I’ve had a very nice career of it.
